title: 'Muggles' and tea in the jazz world
summary: He explains the terms muggle and tea, Mezzrow, and his own limited use.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: We were talking about smoking pot informally before we, well we're still informal for that matter, but I mean before we turned the tape on we were talking about it. And you said, oh, boy I've got a funny story about Louis.

Oh yes. Well anyone who has read about Milton Mezzrow, he was a guy hanging around. He didn't play too well. He played the clarinet and saxophone but he always, he used to go out to Arizona and pick up some mighty fine tea, we used to call it. Tea. And it was a cigarette what we would be called a muggles. It was a muggle.
Isn't that funny. You know I have never heard that expression until now. I'm familiar with the term reefer, but muggle I have never heard.

Reefer came later. Muggle was what we used to use. Or say have you got any tea? You know, and that's what Louis, we used to call it tea. We would smoke it but not, we wouldn't overdo it you know. We never took anything stronger than that. And even in

those days I'd talk to doctors about it. And they'd say well, it's not habit forming, just don't smoke too much of it and so forth. But I've always, actually I never used to smoke when I was playing because it made my mouth too dry. But after the was over or something like that I would take a few whiffs and feel good. It's better than drinking I think.
